screens.title: Quadrotor Kinematics and Dynamics
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter you will learn how to represent a quadrotor’s position and orientation, derive its equations of motion from first principles, and implement a dynamics simulator. We begin with simple one-dimensional vertical dynamics, extend to a two-dimensional tilt-and-thrust model, and then review the full three-dimensional Newton–Euler formulation. You will also see how four rotor thrusts map to a total upward force and three rotational torques, and why that mapping makes quadrotors underactuated. Throughout, we point out practical issues like gimbal lock and why quaternions are preferred in production. A concrete outcome: by the end you will be able to write a MATLAB function for use with ode45 that simulates a quadrotor and use it to test controllers that hover or follow a trajectory. Think about a hover example: applying just enough thrust to equal weight keeps altitude constant; this simple fact drives both simulation checks and controller design. As you explore, ask yourself: when must the vehicle tilt to move horizontally, and what does that coupling imply for control?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Checks
screens.narratorSegment: These skill checks focus your practice and reveal common pitfalls. First, check your modeling by converting a body-frame thrust vector with a rotation matrix and confirming the inertial acceleration matches expected hover behavior. Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Learning Objectives — Skills & Checks
Skills & verification steps
  • Model check: rotate a body thrust into the world frame and confirm p̈ when u = m·g equals zero.

screens.title: Quadrotor platform and state definition
screens.narratorSegment: Start by defining the vehicle and its state. A quadrotor is a four-rotor helicopter in a cross configuration. Physically it is simple, but dynamically it is underactuated: four independent motor thrusts control one total upward force and three torques, while the vehicle has six degrees of freedom in space. We record the system state using twelve variables: three positions (x, y, z), three linear velocities, three orientation angles (commonly roll, pitch, yaw), and three angular velocity components. This twelve-dimensional state is the minimal set needed to predict future motion under given motor inputs. A concrete example: if the vehicle tilts forward, the body-z thrust vector rotates in the world frame and produces acceleration along x and z simultaneously. A common misconception is to think that adding more sensors increases control authority; sensors help estimate the state but do not add actuators. Another misunderstanding is to confuse underactuation with instability; an underactuated system can be stable but cannot arbitrarily control all degrees of freedom independently. Key takeaway: the twelve-variable state fully captures position and rotation dynamics you will derive in the next screens.

keyIdea.title: State vector
keyIdea.text: Position, velocity, orientation, and angular rates form a 12-variable state needed for dynamics and control.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Quadrotor platform and state definition
Quadrotor and underactuation
Four rotors, six degrees of freedom — tilt to translate.
State definition
x, y, z — position; vx, vy, vz — linear velocity; roll, pitch, yaw — orientation; ωx, ωy, ωz — angular velocity.
Why twelve?
You need both configuration and rates to form a first-order ordinary differential equation system. Integration of these rates predicts future pose and motion under inputs.
Misconception check
More sensors don't increase actuation. Underactuation is about actuators, not observability. A system can be observable and still underactuated.
Key Takeaway

The full state includes pose and rates; controllers and simulators must propagate all twelve variables to predict motion correctly.

Concrete example
Imagine a hover where motor commands change so the vehicle tilts by five degrees pitch. The body z-axis thrust is rotated, producing a forward acceleration component. That forward acceleration appears in the vx equation even though only thrust changed; orientation and translation are coupled.
State quick reference
Position: x, y, z
Velocity: vx, vy, vz
Angles: roll, pitch, yaw
Angular rates: ωx, ωy, ωz
Question to reflect on: given these twelve variables, which can you control directly with motor thrusts, and which only indirectly through attitude changes?

screens.title: From four rotor thrusts to total thrust and torques
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding how motor thrusts map to vehicle forces is essential. The four rotors produce individual thrusts u1, u2, u3, u4. The total upward thrust u equals the sum of all four thrusts; this is what counteracts gravity in the vertical equation. Roll torque is generated by the left–right thrust difference, typically proportional to (u2 + u3) − (u1 + u4) depending on your rotor labeling. Pitch torque arises from the front–back difference, proportional to (u1 + u2) − (u3 + u4) in a common labeling. Yaw torque is generated by rotor reaction: rotors spinning clockwise create a reaction opposite to those spinning counterclockwise. Two rotors spin each way so when their speeds differ, a net yaw moment appears. A concrete numeric example: if left rotors are increased by 0.1 N and right decreased by 0.1 N, the net thrust may remain constant while a roll torque is produced. Common mistake: assuming each rotor independently controls a single axis. In reality, a change in one motor affects total thrust and may require rebalancing other rotors to achieve pure torque without changing lift. The mapping is linear in small-angle models, and understanding it lets you build decoupling controllers or mix motor commands from desired collective thrust and torques.

keyIdea.title: Motor mapping
keyIdea.text: Total thrust is the sum of rotor thrusts; torques are differences between rotor groups and depend on rotor rotation directions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Motor inputs → forces
Linear mapping of inputs
Define motor thrusts u1..u4. Compute collective and differential commands for thrust and torques.
Equations (concept)
Total thrust u = u1 + u2 + u3 + u4. Roll torque τx ∝ (left side thrusts) − (right side thrusts). Pitch torque τy ∝ (front) − (back). Yaw τz arises from rotor reaction signs.
Concrete example
If u1=1.0, u2=1.0, u3=1.0, u4=1.0 then u=4.0 and no torques. If u1 and u4 are reduced by 0.1 and u2 and u3 increased by 0.1, u stays 4.0 but a roll torque appears.
Misconception
Adjusting a single rotor changes thrust and torques simultaneously. To create pure torque you must offset thrust changes among rotors so the total stays constant.
Mixer visualization
Collective: u = Σ ui
Roll: difference left vs right
Pitch: difference front vs back
Yaw: rotor spin imbalance
Key Takeaway

Motor mixing turns desired thrust and torques into four motor commands; understanding the mix is essential for control and for preserving altitude while commanding rotation.

screens.title: 1D vertical dynamics
screens.narratorSegment: We begin with the simplest useful model: vertical motion only. In this one-dimensional model the vehicle moves only along z and the single control is the total thrust u. Newton's second law gives m times vertical acceleration equals the upward thrust minus gravity: m · z̈ = u − m · g. This is a second-order linear ordinary differential equation. Practically, this means when u is greater than m·g the vehicle accelerates upward, when u is less it accelerates downward, and when u equals m·g it hovers. A concrete use case is testing a basic altitude controller: choose a thrust command equal to m·g plus a proportional term on altitude error and watch how the system converges. A common misconception is to treat thrust as an instantaneous velocity command; instead thrust produces acceleration, and controllers must integrate acceleration to get position. When simulating, ensure units are consistent: thrust in newtons, mass in kilograms, gravity in meters per second squared. Takeaway: the vertical equation captures the essence of altitude control and is the simplest equation you will implement and verify before moving to tilt-coupled motion.

keyIdea.title: 1D equation
keyIdea.text: m·z̈ = u − m·g, a second-order system: thrust controls acceleration, not velocity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › 1D vertical dynamics
Vertical motion model
m · z̈ = u − m · g — the basis for altitude control.
Interpretation
Thrust produces acceleration. Controllers must command thrust so the integrated acceleration yields the desired position profile.
Example: simple hover controller
Set u = m·g + Kp·(z_des − z). If Kp is small this yields gradual correction; if large it can overshoot. Use a derivative or integral term to tune performance.
Key Takeaway

Altitude control is a second-order problem: design controllers that convert position error into a thrust that safely produces required acceleration.

Simulation note
When you simulate this equation with ode45, integrate z and ż as state variables and apply u(t). Start by validating hover: constant u = m·g should keep ż constant at zero.
Misconception
Treating thrust as a direct position command leads to poor controllers. Always remember thrust changes acceleration, then integrate.

screens.title: 2D tilt-and-thrust dynamics
screens.narratorSegment: Extending to two dimensions reveals the key coupling between attitude and horizontal motion. In a 2D model we keep x and z plus a single rotation θ for pitch. The equations are ẍ = (u / m) · sin(θ), z̈ = (u / m) · cos(θ) − g, and θ̈ = τ / Iy, where τ is pitch torque and Iy the rotational inertia about the pitch axis. The crucial point: horizontal acceleration ẍ arises because the thrust vector is tilted by θ. Practically, to move forward a quadrotor increases thrust and tilts forward; the forward acceleration is proportional to sin(θ) times thrust over mass. A concrete scenario: to travel from x=0 to x=5 meters while keeping z≈2 meters, the controller first increases pitch slightly and keeps thrust near m·g so the forward acceleration is small and controlled. A common misconception is to expect horizontal motion without tilt; that would require a horizontal thruster, which quadrotors lack. Pay attention to the torque equation: angular acceleration depends on applied torque and moment of inertia, so the pitch response is slower for larger inertia. Takeaway: lateral motion is inherently attitude-coupled and control must manage both thrust and torque together.

keyIdea.title: 2D coupling
keyIdea.text: Horizontal acceleration requires tilt: ẍ scales with (u/m)·sin(θ), so attitude and thrust must be coordinated for motion.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › 2D tilt-and-thrust dynamics
2D dynamics equations
ẍ = (u/m)·sin(θ); z̈ = (u/m)·cos(θ) − g; θ̈ = τ / Iy.
Example trajectory
Start at x=0, z=2. To reach x=5, command a positive pitch and maintain thrust near m·g. To stop, pitch back to create negative acceleration and then level out.
Control implication
Controllers must coordinate torque commands (to change θ) and thrust commands (to control magnitude of acceleration). Separate loops for attitude and position are common, with position commanding desired pitch.
Misconception
Assuming thrust alone moves horizontally ignores geometry. Horizontal force is created by reorienting the same thrust vector.
Annotated step cards
Step 1 — Attitude change
Apply τ to change θ according to θ̈ = τ/Iy.
Step 2 — Thrust
Collective thrust u projects into horizontal via sin(θ).
Step 3 — Position update
Integrate ẍ and z̈ to update velocities and positions in simulation.
Reflect: how does a heavier vehicle (larger m) change the required pitch or thrust for the same horizontal acceleration?

screens.title: 3D Newton–Euler dynamics
screens.narratorSegment: The full three-dimensional model combines Newton’s law for translation and Euler’s equations for rotation. Translational dynamics in the inertial frame are m·p̈ = R · [0; 0; u] − [0; 0; m·g], where p is position and R maps the body frame thrust into the world. Rotational dynamics in the body frame follow I·ω̇ = τ − ω × (I·ω). Here I is the inertia matrix, ω is the angular velocity vector, τ is the torque vector from motors, and the cross product ω × (I·ω) is the gyroscopic torque term. Gyroscopic effects arise from spinning rotors and can be significant for agile maneuvers; for slow flight you may neglect them as a simplifying assumption. A concrete example: during a fast yaw rotation, gyroscopic coupling can introduce unexpected roll or pitch moments if unmodeled. A common misconception is to think rotation and translation are independent; R couples them because thrust expressed in body coordinates must be rotated to inertial coordinates. For simulation and control, implement R carefully, check units, and include or omit gyroscopic torque based on expected maneuvering speeds. Final takeaway: Newton–Euler is compact but hides important cross-coupling terms you must consider when moving beyond gentle flight.

keyIdea.text: m·p̈ = R·[0;0;u] − [0;0;m·g]; I·ω̇ = τ − ω×(I·ω). Rotation matrix R couples attitude to translational forces.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › 3D Newton–Euler dynamics
Translational dynamics
m · p̈ = R · [0; 0; u] − [0; 0; m·g]. Rotation matrix R maps body thrust into the world.
Rotational dynamics
I · ω̇ = τ − ω × (I · ω). The cross term is gyroscopic torque from angular momentum coupling.
When to include gyroscopic term
Include it for agile, fast rotations where rotor spin and body rotation interact; neglect it for gentle hover to simplify the model.
Practical checks
  • Verify R is constructed using the same Euler convention as transforms you use elsewhere.
  • Confirm units for I, τ, and ω are consistent (N·m, rad/s, kg·m²).
  • Test simple motions: pure thrust, pure torque, and combined inputs to validate coupling.
Key Takeaway

Newton–Euler captures full coupling; rotation matrices move forces between frames and gyroscopic terms capture cross-coupling from spinning rotors.

screens.title: Euler angles vs quaternions
screens.narratorSegment: Rotation representation is a practical choice with consequences. Euler angles (roll, pitch, yaw) are intuitive and easy to visualize, which makes them useful for classroom derivations and quick controllers. However, Euler angles suffer from gimbal lock: when pitch reaches ±90 degrees, two rotation axes align and you lose a degree of freedom numerically. This creates singularities that can destabilize computations or confuse controllers near those attitudes. Quaternions are a four-parameter alternative that represent rotations without singularities. They consist of a scalar and a three-vector and map cleanly to rotation matrices. A concrete contrast: if your quadrotor flips end-over-end, Euler angles may produce a discontinuous jump or rapidly changing derivatives, while quaternions remain smooth. A common misconception is that quaternions are magically better in every case; they require normalization and careful numeric handling, but avoid gimbal lock and are preferred for production flight stacks. Takeaway: use Euler angles for simple derivations and visualization, but adopt quaternions for robust simulation and control when large rotations are possible. Euler angles vs quaternions means euler angles are intuitive but can gimbal lock; quaternions avoid singularities and are preferred for robust systems.. In practical terms, why euler angles are intuitive but quaternions avoid gimbal lock. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Euler angles vs quaternions
Comparison table
Euler angles
Intuitive, three parameters; suffer from singularities (gimbal lock) at certain attitudes.
Quaternions
Four parameters, no singularity, smooth interpolation; must normalize to avoid drift.
When to use which
Euler for derivations and small angles; quaternions for full 3D flight and production simulators.
Concrete example
If pitch approaches 90 degrees, Euler-based control can behave erratically because roll and yaw become indistinguishable. With quaternions you can represent that same orientation without losing a degree of freedom.
Misconception
Quaternions are not human-readable angles; they require conversion to visualize, but they give numerical robustness for controllers and simulators.
Key Takeaway

Use Euler angles for intuition; use quaternions for reliability when rotations approach singular configurations.

screens.title: MATLAB dynamics function for ode45

keyIdea.title: Implement dynamics
keyIdea.text: Organize the 12-state vector, build R consistently, compute translational and rotational derivatives, and test with ode45.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › MATLAB dynamics for ode45
Key implementation points
Organize the state vector, compute R with a consistent convention, and return derivatives in the correct order for ode45.
<% MATLAB pseudo-code snippet displayed for clarity >
function dxdt = quadrotor_dynamics(t, x, u, m, g, I)
  % State: [x;y;z; vx;vy;vz; roll;pitch;yaw; wx;wy;wz]
  p = x(1:3);
  v = x(4:6);
  angles = x(7:9);
  w = x(10:12);

  % Rotation matrix (ZYX Euler example)
  R = eul2rotm(angles', 'ZYX');

  u_total = u(1);
  tau = u(2:4);

  dpdt = v;
  dvdt = (R * [0;0;u_total] - [0;0;m*g]) / m;

  danglesdt = w;
  dwdt = I \ tau; % simplified rotational dynamics

  dxdt = [dpdt; dvdt; danglesdt; dwdt];
end
Implementation tips
  • Pass m and I as parameters to avoid magic numbers.
  • Check eul2rotm ordering. ZYX is common for yaw-pitch-roll conventions.
  • Normalize quaternions if you switch to quaternion-based rotations.
Key Takeaway

A clear state layout and consistent rotation conventions are the most common sources of errors in dynamics code. Validate with simple hover tests first.

screens.title: Controller for hover and trajectory experiments
screens.narratorSegment: Use simple controllers to validate your dynamics model. For hover at z = 2 meters, a baseline controller sets total thrust to m·g plus a proportional correction on altitude error: u = m·g + Kp_z · (z_des − z). For attitude, use a PD controller on angles so the vehicle stays near θ = 0 while maintaining altitude. To move horizontally to x = 5 meters, implement a position controller that commands a desired pitch angle based on x error. Concretely, compute θ_des = Kp_x · (x_des − x), then command τ to drive θ toward θ_des. Simulate with ode45 for ten seconds using m = 0.5 kg, Iy = 0.01 kg·m², and g = 9.81; plot x versus z to observe the curved trajectory produced by tilt and thrust. A common mistake is commanding too large θ_des and causing aggressive forward acceleration and overshoot; tune gains conservatively. Another pitfall is neglecting integral action for steady-state offset; if you see a persistent altitude error, add an integral term. Takeaway: build nested loops—position to attitude to motor mix—and test step responses before more complex trajectories.

keyIdea.text: Position loop commands desired attitude; attitude loop commands torques; thrust loop maintains altitude. Tune conservatively and validate with simple steps.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Controller for hover and trajectory
Hover controller
u = m·g + Kp_z·(z_des − z) plus attitude PD to keep roll/pitch near zero.
Position → Attitude
Compute desired pitch from x error: θ_des = Kp_x·(x_des − x). Send θ_des to attitude controller.
Tuning tips
Start with small gains to avoid overshoot. Validate hover before enabling horizontal motion. Add integral action if steady-state errors persist.
Simulation exercise
Parameters: m = 0.5 kg, Iy = 0.01 kg·m², g = 9.81 m/s². Simulate 10 seconds, plot x vs z, and observe how the quadrotor must pitch forward to accelerate, then pitch back to stop.
Key Takeaway

Nested control loops that map position error to attitude commands and attitude error to torque are standard. Validate with step tests and gradually enable more aggressive maneuvers.

screens.title: 2D simulation lab and assessment idea
screens.narratorSegment: The hands-on activity asks you to write a 2D simulator using ode45 and test two experiments: maintain hover at z = 2 meters and move from x = 0 to x = 5 while maintaining altitude. Use parameters m = 0.5 kg, Iy = 0.01 kg·m², g = 9.81 m/s². Implement a dynamics function that returns derivatives for x, z, θ and their rates, using the equations ẍ = (u/m)·sin(θ), z̈ = (u/m)·cos(θ) − g, and θ̈ = τ / Iy. For the hover controller apply u = m·g plus a small proportional correction on altitude error and zero torque for attitude, then enable a small attitude controller to hold θ = 0. A useful assessment question: explain why the quadrotor is underactuated and give a step-by-step account of how you produced forward motion in your simulation. A common error in student code is attempting to control x directly by setting ẍ—this bypasses dynamics and produces unrealistic results. Takeaway: the lab consolidates modeling, control, and simulation practice and makes the underactuation concept concrete through plotted trajectories.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › 2D simulation lab
Lab instructions
Implement a 2D dynamics function for ode45 and run two experiments: a hover at z=2 m and a horizontal motion to x=5 m while maintaining altitude.
Parameters
m = 0.5 kg, Iy = 0.01 kg·m², g = 9.81 m/s². Simulate for 10 seconds and plot x vs z.
Assessment question
Why is the quadrotor underactuated? Use your simulation results to explain how tilt generates horizontal acceleration and why direct control of x is impossible with only rotor thrusts.
Common pitfalls
  • Forgetting to include gravity in z̈.
  • Using inconsistent Euler order for rotation matrix construction.

The lab turns theoretical equations into measurable trajectories and clarifies underactuation through practical controller design and plots.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Summarizing the essentials helps retention. Remember that a quadrotor uses four rotors to produce one total thrust and three torques, which makes it underactuated: it cannot command all six degrees of freedom independently. The 1D vertical equation m·z̈ = u − m·g explains altitude control; in 2D, horizontal acceleration appears via tilting so ẍ = (u/m)·sin(θ). In 3D, the Newton–Euler pair m·p̈ = R·[0;0;u] − [0;0;m·g] and I·ω̇ = τ − ω×(I·ω) capture translation and rotation. Euler angles are intuitive but can gimbal lock; quaternions avoid that singularity and are preferred for production. Finally, implementing dynamics in MATLAB for ode45 requires consistent state ordering, rotation conventions, and careful testing with hover and simple trajectories. These core ideas connect modeling, simulation, and controller design and form the foundation for more advanced flight dynamics work.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you will learn how to represent a quadrotor’s position and orientation, derive its equations of motion from first principles, and implement a dynamics simulator. We begin with simple one-dimensional vertical dynamics, extend to a two-dimensional tilt-and-thrust model, and then review the full three-dimensional Newton–Euler formulation. You will also see how four rotor thrusts map to a total upward force and three rotational torques, and why that mapping makes quadrotors underactuated. Throughout, we point out practical issues like gimbal lock and why quaternions are preferred in production. A concrete outcome: by the end you will be able to write a MATLAB function for use with ode45 that simulates a quadrotor and use it to test controllers that hover or follow a trajectory. Think about a hover example: applying just enough thrust to equal weight keeps altitude constant; this simple fact drives both simulation checks and controller design. As you explore, ask yourself: when must the vehicle tilt to move horizontally, and what does that coupling imply for control?

These objectives guide practice and assessment. First, you will model a quadrotor’s 3D pose using rotation matrices and homogeneous transforms; this means writing a rotation matrix that converts body-frame thrust vectors into inertial accelerations and using transforms to position the vehicle. Second, you will derive motion equations across 1D, 2D, and 3D: you should be able to show the vertical second-order equation, the 2D tilt-and-thrust equations, and the Newton–Euler translational and rotational dynamics. Third, you will explain how individual motor thrusts map into total thrust and three torques, and how that mapping creates underactuation that forces tilt for horizontal motion. Fourth, you will implement a MATLAB dynamics function for use with ode45, run simulations, and interpret trajectories. Each objective includes practical checks: write the equations, simulate a hover, and explain why Euler angles can cause gimbal lock. These skills matter because they let you validate controllers in simulation before flight and reason about stability and maneuverability in real vehicles.

These skill checks focus your practice and reveal common pitfalls. First, check your modeling by converting a body-frame thrust vector with a rotation matrix and confirming the inertial acceleration matches expected hover behavior. Second, derive the vertical equation and simulate it: when the total thrust equals mass times gravity, the vertical acceleration is zero and the vehicle hovers. Third, verify torque decomposition by writing the expressions for roll, pitch, and yaw torques in terms of motor thrust differences and rotor directions. Fourth, implement the provided MATLAB function signature, run ode45, and validate trajectories for a hover and a forward reach. Watch out for misconceptions: Euler angles are fine for classroom derivations but can fail near pitch of ±90 degrees — that’s gimbal lock. For robust numerical work, test quaternion conversions and check that your inertia matrix and gyroscopic terms are correctly implemented. These checks ensure a simulator that behaves like the physics you derived.

Start by defining the vehicle and its state. A quadrotor is a four-rotor helicopter in a cross configuration. Physically it is simple, but dynamically it is underactuated: four independent motor thrusts control one total upward force and three torques, while the vehicle has six degrees of freedom in space. We record the system state using twelve variables: three positions (x, y, z), three linear velocities, three orientation angles (commonly roll, pitch, yaw), and three angular velocity components. This twelve-dimensional state is the minimal set needed to predict future motion under given motor inputs. A concrete example: if the vehicle tilts forward, the body-z thrust vector rotates in the world frame and produces acceleration along x and z simultaneously. A common misconception is to think that adding more sensors increases control authority; sensors help estimate the state but do not add actuators. Another misunderstanding is to confuse underactuation with instability; an underactuated system can be stable but cannot arbitrarily control all degrees of freedom independently. Key takeaway: the twelve-variable state fully captures position and rotation dynamics you will derive in the next screens.

Understanding how motor thrusts map to vehicle forces is essential. The four rotors produce individual thrusts u1, u2, u3, u4. The total upward thrust u equals the sum of all four thrusts; this is what counteracts gravity in the vertical equation. Roll torque is generated by the left–right thrust difference, typically proportional to (u2 + u3) − (u1 + u4) depending on your rotor labeling. Pitch torque arises from the front–back difference, proportional to (u1 + u2) − (u3 + u4) in a common labeling. Yaw torque is generated by rotor reaction: rotors spinning clockwise create a reaction opposite to those spinning counterclockwise. Two rotors spin each way so when their speeds differ, a net yaw moment appears. A concrete numeric example: if left rotors are increased by 0.1 N and right decreased by 0.1 N, the net thrust may remain constant while a roll torque is produced. Common mistake: assuming each rotor independently controls a single axis. In reality, a change in one motor affects total thrust and may require rebalancing other rotors to achieve pure torque without changing lift. The mapping is linear in small-angle models, and understanding it lets you build decoupling controllers or mix motor commands from desired collective thrust and torques.

We begin with the simplest useful model: vertical motion only. In this one-dimensional model the vehicle moves only along z and the single control is the total thrust u. Newton's second law gives m times vertical acceleration equals the upward thrust minus gravity: m · z̈ = u − m · g. This is a second-order linear ordinary differential equation. Practically, this means when u is greater than m·g the vehicle accelerates upward, when u is less it accelerates downward, and when u equals m·g it hovers. A concrete use case is testing a basic altitude controller: choose a thrust command equal to m·g plus a proportional term on altitude error and watch how the system converges. A common misconception is to treat thrust as an instantaneous velocity command; instead thrust produces acceleration, and controllers must integrate acceleration to get position. When simulating, ensure units are consistent: thrust in newtons, mass in kilograms, gravity in meters per second squared. Takeaway: the vertical equation captures the essence of altitude control and is the simplest equation you will implement and verify before moving to tilt-coupled motion.

Extending to two dimensions reveals the key coupling between attitude and horizontal motion. In a 2D model we keep x and z plus a single rotation θ for pitch. The equations are ẍ = (u / m) · sin(θ), z̈ = (u / m) · cos(θ) − g, and θ̈ = τ / Iy, where τ is pitch torque and Iy the rotational inertia about the pitch axis. The crucial point: horizontal acceleration ẍ arises because the thrust vector is tilted by θ. Practically, to move forward a quadrotor increases thrust and tilts forward; the forward acceleration is proportional to sin(θ) times thrust over mass. A concrete scenario: to travel from x=0 to x=5 meters while keeping z≈2 meters, the controller first increases pitch slightly and keeps thrust near m·g so the forward acceleration is small and controlled. A common misconception is to expect horizontal motion without tilt; that would require a horizontal thruster, which quadrotors lack. Pay attention to the torque equation: angular acceleration depends on applied torque and moment of inertia, so the pitch response is slower for larger inertia. Takeaway: lateral motion is inherently attitude-coupled and control must manage both thrust and torque together.

The full three-dimensional model combines Newton’s law for translation and Euler’s equations for rotation. Translational dynamics in the inertial frame are m·p̈ = R · [0; 0; u] − [0; 0; m·g], where p is position and R maps the body frame thrust into the world. Rotational dynamics in the body frame follow I·ω̇ = τ − ω × (I·ω). Here I is the inertia matrix, ω is the angular velocity vector, τ is the torque vector from motors, and the cross product ω × (I·ω) is the gyroscopic torque term. Gyroscopic effects arise from spinning rotors and can be significant for agile maneuvers; for slow flight you may neglect them as a simplifying assumption. A concrete example: during a fast yaw rotation, gyroscopic coupling can introduce unexpected roll or pitch moments if unmodeled. A common misconception is to think rotation and translation are independent; R couples them because thrust expressed in body coordinates must be rotated to inertial coordinates. For simulation and control, implement R carefully, check units, and include or omit gyroscopic torque based on expected maneuvering speeds. Final takeaway: Newton–Euler is compact but hides important cross-coupling terms you must consider when moving beyond gentle flight.

Rotation representation is a practical choice with consequences. Euler angles (roll, pitch, yaw) are intuitive and easy to visualize, which makes them useful for classroom derivations and quick controllers. However, Euler angles suffer from gimbal lock: when pitch reaches ±90 degrees, two rotation axes align and you lose a degree of freedom numerically. This creates singularities that can destabilize computations or confuse controllers near those attitudes. Quaternions are a four-parameter alternative that represent rotations without singularities. They consist of a scalar and a three-vector and map cleanly to rotation matrices. A concrete contrast: if your quadrotor flips end-over-end, Euler angles may produce a discontinuous jump or rapidly changing derivatives, while quaternions remain smooth. A common misconception is that quaternions are magically better in every case; they require normalization and careful numeric handling, but avoid gimbal lock and are preferred for production flight stacks. Takeaway: use Euler angles for simple derivations and visualization, but adopt quaternions for robust simulation and control when large rotations are possible.
